name: M365 offboarding auditor — the join two separate reports cannot make
_why: The business case for an agent, stated as a test. Offboarding is three jobs
in two systems: disable the account, release the licence, remove the mail
routing. Each has a report; none knows about the others. A leaver disabled
on day one looks finished in the system that did it while their seat bills
for a year and their inbox forwards to a personal address the whole time.
What is pinned here is that the agent leads with the LEAK — a disabled
account whose rule is still enabled and still hiding itself — rather than
with the bigger-looking licence number, and that it reports licences as
SEATS and SKU names with no invented currency figure, because Microsoft
does not publish what a tenant pays.
It also pins the honest closing line: the sweep covered disabled accounts
only, so a clean result here is not a clean result for the tenant.

tools.name: workflow_61
tools.description: Lists every subscribed SKU with prepaid against assigned seats, and every user with the licences they hold, whether their account is still enabled and when they last signed in. Read-only.

tools.name: workflow_63
tools.description: Finds inbox rules that forward or redirect mail to addresses outside the organisation, and flags the ones that also mark as read, move or delete the original. Read-only.

event.input: We had a round of leavers last quarter. Were they actually offboarded?

value.restated: Check whether the people who left have been fully offboarded: account disabled, licence released, and no mail routing left behind.
observations_needed: Which disabled accounts still hold licences, and which SKUs
Which disabled accounts still have inbox rules forwarding mail externally

script.text: Taking both audits together — neither answers the offboarding question alone.

script.text: Both audits returned and they overlap on two people.

findings.summary: j.okafor@customer.com is disabled but an enabled inbox rule still forwards mail to a personal outlook.com address and marks the original as read — a rule that conceals itself was not set up for convenience.
s.varga@customer.com is disabled but an enabled rule still redirects mail to a personal gmail.com address.
14 disabled accounts still hold licences, 14 seats in total, and a further 6 paid seats have never been assigned to anyone.
3 licensed accounts have never signed in, including one that looks like a service account by its name — these need classifying by someone who knows the tenant, not reclaiming.

script.text:
**Two people who left are still forwarding mail out of the company, and 14 disabled accounts are still holding licences [e:701][e:702].**

Still leaking — deal with these first:

- j.okafor@customer.com is disabled, and an enabled inbox rule still forwards to a personal outlook.com address and marks the original as read [e:702]. A rule that hides itself was not set up for convenience.
- s.varga@customer.com is disabled, and an enabled rule still redirects to a personal gmail.com address [e:702].

One further rule on r.mensah@customer.com points at a partner domain and is already disabled, so it is housekeeping rather than exposure [e:702].

Still billing:

| SKU | Prepaid | Assigned | Unassigned |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SPE_E5 | 120 | 116 | 4 [e:701] |
| SPB | 40 | 38 | 2 [e:701] |

Fourteen seats are assigned to disabled accounts, and a further six paid seats have never been assigned to anyone [e:701]. I have no prices — Microsoft does not publish what this tenant pays, and it varies by agreement — so the seat counts are what to take to the renewal conversation.

To review rather than reclaim:

- Three licensed accounts have never signed in, one of them named svc-scanner [e:701]. Shared mailboxes and service accounts look identical to leavers in this data, so somebody who knows the tenant should classify these before anything is removed.

Recommended order: remove the two live forwarding rules first, then release the licences and convert those mailboxes to shared. Do not delete the accounts — that loses the mailbox, the OneDrive and the audit trail, which most retention obligations require you to keep.

Not checked: the mailbox sweep covered disabled accounts only, so an active employee forwarding company mail externally would not appear in this report.
